I recently sold a Coherent Sapphire 200 mW blue laser to Bishop's University for their holography lab. They made some coherence length measurements I thought might be of interest here. 

**Coherent 215M laser 8 meters minimum (the 315M’s should be the same or better).**

**Coherent Sapphire laser (running SLM) 9 meters minimum**

For this reason I will test and laser I sell here on the forum very thoroughly on my Spectra Physics 2 GHz FSR scanning interferometer. See the for sale page for the tested blue lasers. Best wishes, Phil, 142laser

> **DJM:** I´ve been told that the Coherent Sapphire lasers switch between SLM and MLM, and that they are in SLM in about 90% of the time.

That's interesting. If true, it's about the same thing as using a diode laser and hoping that is doesn't mode-hop during an exposure. People often speak of coherence length, but a laser can have a long coherence length for short and/or erratic time periods, which will wreak havoc as far as holography is concerned. A more meaningful specification would be something like "5 meters coherence length over 5 hours."

posts.author: 142laser
posts.content_md:
IHi,

Sapphire was designed to be SLM and the early articles on the OPSL design technology all claimed SLM output. However once production started it was observed that some units ran MLM and that some flipped between SLM and MLM so the claim of SLM was dropped. There is no way for a company like Coherent doing high volume production can test each laser head for 2-3 days and 20 power cycles on a scanning interferometer; the additional cost would be ridiculous. But I can do that and from what I have seen it is highly probable that the well behaved lasers will be useable for holography through their lifetime if not overheated or abused. I have tested two Sapphire HP 200 mW heads and four 200 mW MP heads (same form factor as LP but up to 200 mW spec) and only one of the six units ran MLM; none were flippers. I base my comments here on test results and NOT on what I hear people say.

Now if you just buy a used Sapphire off e Bay that has not been tested for SLM you may get a MLM head or a "flipper". This is why you have heard bad things; when a Sapphire is running SLM it is an ideal holography laser, great beam, great stability and ~9 meter coherence length. The new Sapphire SF heads are just coming out and it will be years before any show up used on e Bay so buying a well tested unit is a good alternative in the meantime. 

I will report on the next batch of Sapphire 488-20 lasers that I test in the next couple weeks. Some will be SLM and available for purchase at a reasonable cost. Best wishes for bright, clear holograms.

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
> **142laser:** the "real" useable coherence length is usually limited by vibration.

No. All "coherence length" is limited by vibration, or none of it is, because vibration causes a displacement of the fringes, and so reduces modulaiton.The fringe modulation is dependant on the interbeam angle and given by the Michelson visibility function, which is independent of the coherence length. So, the amount of vibration that destroys a shot depends on whether the maximum of the fringe moves into an area where the the minimum of the fringe was. In other words, whether I_max - I_min is itself maximised. Whether you have a coherence length of millimetres or kilometres, so long as you're within the coherence length, a blur creating a displacement of x will alter the fringe position by kx (k=2*pi/lambda). If kx<pi, you're OK, if not, you get weak holograms. As you depart from exactly equal path lengths, the fringe modulation drops until, as the path length difference veers towards the edge of the coherence length, the fringe modulation reduces to zero. The actual modulation fall-off is a sinc-squared curve, however, for all practical purposes, roughly being off by about 1/3rd of the coherence length will give you good fringes.

Taking a concrete example, let's say you have a laser of coherence length 10cm and you're shooting with a HeNe at an interbeam angle of 30 degrees. Then the fringe density is 790 l/mm, or the fringe maxima occur at 1.2 microns. In this case, k=2*pi/lambda ~ 10, so to move a "light" part of the fringe into a "dark" part of the fringe (total loss in modulation), you'd have to have a motion of 0.3 microns. This is completely independant of the coherence length. The coherence length depends only on the bandwidth and is given by

L = (lambda)^2/delta(lambda)

and so long as your path difference are less than about 3 cm, the fringe modulation, or the distances between maxima and minima of the fringe structure is independent of the coherence length

One curious fact that is not well known is to remember that the modulation curve of the coherence length is a sinc-squared curve. This means that the modulation falls off to zero at some interpath difference,*then rises again*, then falls again and then rises again. It never rises to it's full height, in fact the second maximum is only 0.04 of the first maximum. I actually exploited this little known fact in a project many moons ago.

posts.author: 142laser
posts.content_md:
That is very detailed and correct. My point is with a coherence length of say 9 meters you really don't need to even worry about path length difference on a table of reasonable size. When using HeNe's and other coherence limited sources it is imperative or one will get weak or nonexistent holograms. I have also seen the modes come back into coherence at a longer distance but this only happens (in a reasonable distance) with 3 or 4 modes. So if you have a pure SLM laser and a quiet table you should have very good fringe contrast with proper setup. 

Coherent 215M, 315M and also specially selected and tested Sapphire lasers can give you this long coherence length and they are commonly available on the used market here and on e bay. JDS “Microgreens” are also typically SLM. Be wary of Sapphires unless the seller has tested the laser for SLM over many hours and days; they can also run MLM or flip. Phil, 142laser
